title: A New Bill Wants to Kill the H-1B Lottery and End OPT. Indian Tech Workers Are in the Crosshairs.
excerpt: Republican Chip Roy's American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act would replace the visa lottery with a wage-based system, ban companies that laid off workers from hiring H-1B holders, and abolish the OPT program that hundreds of thousands of Indian students rely on.
body:
Republican Texas Representative Chip Roy has introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026, a sweeping bill that would fundamentally reshape the H-1B visa program and abolish the Optional Practical Training pathway that has served as a lifeline for hundreds of thousands of Indian students and workers in the United States.

The legislation, introduced on June 4 with backing from Representative Eli Crane of Arizona, takes direct aim at the lottery system that currently governs H-1B visa allocation. In its place, Roy proposes a wage-based selection process that would prioritize higher-paid applicants, require employers to demonstrate good-faith efforts to recruit American workers first, and bar companies that have conducted recent layoffs from sponsoring H-1B visas altogether.

"For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favor of cheap foreign labor, while masking layoffs and wage suppression as 'shortages,'" Roy said in a statement accompanying the bill.

## What the Bill Would Do

The core provisions of the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act read like a checklist of the Indian tech diaspora's worst fears. The bill would require the Department of Labor and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to conduct a labor market test for every H-1B petition, verifying that an employer made a genuine attempt to hire a domestic worker before turning to a foreign applicant. Employers would also be required to pay H-1B workers the same wage as American employees with equivalent experience and qualifications — a provision aimed at closing what critics call the "wage gap loophole" that allows companies to hire cheaper foreign talent.

Perhaps most consequentially for Indian immigrants waiting decades in the green card backlog, the bill would end the use of H-1B visas as a pathway to permanent residency. It would sever a connection that has been a central pillar of immigration planning for Indian professionals — many of whom currently face wait times of 50 years or more for an employment-based green card due to per-country caps.

The bill would also eliminate the Optional Practical Training program entirely. OPT currently allows international graduates from American universities — a disproportionate number of whom are Indian — to work in the United States for up to three years after completing a STEM degree. Abolishing it would shut down one of the most established pipelines for Indian talent entering the American workforce.

## The Scale of What Is at Stake

The bill arrives at a moment when the H-1B program is already under enormous pressure. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin recently told the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee that roughly 286,000 H-1B applications had been filed in fiscal year 2026, with more than 200,000 applicants paying a $100,000 fee for expedited processing. Indian nationals account for approximately 70 percent of all H-1B visas granted annually, making them by far the largest group affected by any reform.

The OPT program is similarly dominated by Indian students. According to federal data, Indian nationals represent the largest share of OPT participants, and the program has become a critical stepping stone to longer-term employment authorization.

U.S. authorities have also recently announced investigations into alleged OPT-related fraud, with officials identifying more than 10,000 students linked to employers they considered suspicious — including cases involving empty offices, shell companies, and unverifiable employment claims. Roy and his supporters cite these investigations as evidence that the program has outlived its purpose.

## Industry and Advocacy Reactions

The bill has drawn swift endorsement from restrictionist organizations. The Federation for American Immigration Reform called it "vital to addressing this abuse" and urged Congress to "stop the flood of cheap foreign labor undermining American talent." Kevin Lynn, president of U.S. Tech Workers, praised the legislation for ensuring "only Congress has the authority to create employment authorization programs."

The Immigration Accountability Project and Citizens for Renewing America have also signed on as supporters.

On the other side, immigration attorneys and tech industry groups have long warned that bills targeting the H-1B program could drive skilled talent to Canada, the United Kingdom, and other countries that are actively competing for the same workers. The National Foundation for American Policy has previously estimated that eliminating the H-1B program would cost the U.S. economy billions in lost productivity and innovation. Canada, in particular, has positioned its Global Talent Stream as a direct alternative, and the UK's High Potential Individual visa has drawn Indian applicants who might once have chosen the American route.

## What Happens Next

Roy's bill builds on Crane's End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026, which proposes a three-year moratorium on all H-1B visa issuances followed by comprehensive reforms. Neither bill is expected to pass quickly — similar proposals have been introduced in previous congressional sessions without reaching a floor vote — but the legislative pressure on H-1B is intensifying with each cycle.

For the roughly 1.5 million Indian professionals and students in the United States whose immigration status is tied in some way to the H-1B or OPT programs, the bill is a reminder that the ground beneath them continues to shift. Even if this particular legislation stalls, the policy direction is unmistakable: the era of unchallenged expansion for skilled-worker visa programs appears to be ending, and the Indian diaspora — which has benefited more than any other group from the system as it exists — will bear the heaviest cost of whatever comes next.
